200 grams (200 g)

*Calculated using standard US customary cup densities. Brown sugar assumes the "packed" method.

How Many Grams in 1 Cup of Sugar?

When a recipe calls for "1 cup of sugar," the gram equivalent depends entirely on which sugar you're using. Granulated white sugar = 200 grams per cup. Brown sugar (packed) = 220 grams per cup. Powdered sugar = just 120 grams per cup. Using the wrong conversion can throw off your sugar ratio by over 60%, so it's worth getting right.

The Conversion Formula (Cups → Grams)

Multiply cups by the grams-per-cup density of your sugar type:

  • Grams = Cups × Grams-per-Cup
  • Granulated Sugar: 1 cup × 200 g/cup = 200 grams
  • Brown Sugar (packed): 1 cup × 220 g/cup = 220 grams
  • Powdered Sugar: 1 cup × 120 g/cup = 120 grams

Why Brown Sugar Is Measured "Packed"

Brown sugar contains molasses, making it inherently moist and prone to air pockets. Recipes that call for brown sugar almost always mean "firmly packed" — pressed into the cup until it holds its shape when turned out. This packing adds roughly 20 extra grams per cup versus the same volume of loose brown sugar. Our converter uses the packed standard (220 g/cup) because that's what virtually all published recipes assume.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q1: How many grams is 1 cup of granulated sugar?

A1: One US customary cup of granulated white sugar weighs exactly 200 grams. This is the universal standard across virtually all baking recipes and conversion charts worldwide.

Q2: Is brown sugar heavier than white sugar per cup?

A2: Yes — when firmly packed as recipes instruct, 1 cup of brown sugar weighs roughly 220 grams, about 20 grams more than granulated white sugar. The molasses content and dense packing account for this difference.

Q3: How does powdered sugar compare to granulated sugar in weight?

A3: One cup of unsifted powdered sugar weighs only ~120 grams, much lighter than granulated sugar's 200 g/cup. If a recipe accidentally swaps these conversions, you'd be off by 80 grams — enough to ruin a frosting or batter.
